code.title: self is passed automatically (Class.method(obj))

followUps:
You get a TypeError at call time, not at definition time. Python still passes the instance as the first argument, so a method defined as def hello(): receives one argument it has no slot for.

Example: Bad().hello() raises TypeError: Bad.hello() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given. The message counts the hidden instance, which confuses beginners who passed nothing. Defining the function is fine; calling it through the class, Bad.hello(), would even work.

Yes, you could, because self is only a convention and the first parameter can have any name. You should not, because every Python tool, linter and reader expects self.

Example: def speak(this): return this.name runs perfectly. But reviewers will stumble, and linters such as pylint flag it (the first-argument naming check). The one accepted exception is cls in class methods and metaclasses, where the first argument is a class, not an instance.

code.title: __new__ vs __init__: uppercase str and a singleton

followUps:
Override __new__, because a str is immutable and its value is fixed when the object is created, so changing it in __init__ is too late.

class Upper(str):
    def __new__(cls, text):
        return super().__new__(cls, text.upper())

Upper("abc")  # 'ABC'

The same applies to int and tuple. Cost is O(n) for the copy of the text; no extra state is kept.

Python skips __init__ entirely, because it only runs __init__ when the returned object is an instance of the class being called.

Example: if Cls.__new__ returns the integer 5, then Cls() evaluates to 5 and Cls.__init__ never runs. If it returns an instance of a subclass of Cls, __init__ does run. This is used by factories and caches, but it surprises readers, so use it sparingly and document it.

code.title: Shared class attribute bug and a correct counter
code.python:
class Bag:
    items = []                        # BUG: one list shared by all
    count = 0
    def add(self, x):
        self.items.append(x)
    def bump(self):
        self.count += 1               # creates instance attribute

a, b = Bag(), Bag()
a.add("apple")
print("b.items:", b.items)            # b sees apple too
a.bump()
print("a.count:", a.count, "Bag.count:", Bag.count)
print("a.__dict__:", a.__dict__)

class Counted:
    total = 0
    def __init__(self):
        type(self).total += 1         # per-class counter (own copy on first use)
class Sub(Counted):
    total = 0
Counted(); Sub(); Sub()
print(Counted.total, Sub.total)

followUps:
Keep the counter on the class and bump it through type(self) (or in __init_subclass__), never through self.

class Base:
    total = 0
    def __init__(self):
        type(self).total += 1
class Sub(Base):
    total = 0   # own counter

With Base(); Sub(); Sub() you get Base.total == 1 and Sub.total == 2. Without total = 0 in Sub, the first += 1 reads Base's value and writes a new Sub attribute that starts from Base's count, so give each subclass its own zero. Each increment is O(1).

A constant is never mutated, so sharing one value among all instances is exactly what you want and it saves memory.

Example: MAX_SIZE = 100 on the class is stored once, whether you create 1 or 1,000,000 objects, and you can change it for all by editing one line. The traps only appear when the shared value is mutable (a list) or when code assigns through an instance. Use an immutable value (number, string, tuple, frozenset) and an UPPER_CASE name to signal it is a constant.

code.title: Attribute lookup order: data descriptor, instance dict, __getattr__
code.python:
class Data:
    def __get__(self, obj, owner): return "data descriptor"
    def __set__(self, obj, v): pass
class NonData:
    def __get__(self, obj, owner): return "non-data descriptor"

class A:
    d = Data()
    n = NonData()
    def __getattr__(self, name):      # only called when normal lookup fails
        return "fallback for " + name

a = A()
a.__dict__["d"] = "instance d"
a.__dict__["n"] = "instance n"
print(a.d)                            # data descriptor wins over instance dict
print(a.n)                            # instance dict wins over non-data
print(a.missing)                      # __getattr__ last
A.plain = 5
print(a.plain)                        # class attribute as is

followUps:
An instance attribute can shadow a method because a function is a non-data descriptor, which loses to the instance dict. A property is a data descriptor (it defines __set__), which wins over the instance dict.

Example: obj.__dict__['hi'] = 5 makes obj.hi return 5, hiding the method hi. But if hi is a property, obj.hi still calls the property, and obj.hi = 5 goes to its setter (or raises AttributeError if there is none).

__getattribute__ runs on every attribute access; __getattr__ runs only as a fallback when normal lookup raised AttributeError.

Example: with __getattr__(self, name) returning a default, obj.x for an existing x never touches it, but obj.missing does. Overriding __getattribute__ is risky: reading self.anything inside it recurses forever, so delegate with object.__getattribute__(self, name). Prefer __getattr__ for proxies and lazy attributes.

code.title: super() follows the MRO in a diamond

followUps:
It breaks the cooperative chain: Parent.__init__(self) always calls that one class, ignoring the MRO, so a shared base can run twice or a sibling can be skipped.

Example: D(B, C), both calling A.__init__(self) directly. Creating D runs A's init twice (once from B, once from C) and C's own init may be skipped by B's direct call. With super().__init__() everywhere, the MRO D, B, C, A runs each class exactly once.

Have each class take the keywords it knows by name, and forward the rest with **kwargs to super().__init__.

class B(A):
    def __init__(self, b=0, **kw):
        super().__init__(**kw)
        self.b = b
# D(a=1, b=2) -> B takes b, A takes a

The last class before object must not forward unknown keywords, otherwise object.__init__ raises TypeError and you see the mistake early. Cost is one dict copy per call, O(k).

code.title: Computing the C3 MRO by hand and a failing case
code.python:
def c3(cls):
    # merge parents' MROs and the parent list (C3 linearization)
    lists = [c3(p) for p in cls.__bases__] + [list(cls.__bases__)]
    result = [cls]
    while any(lists):
        for l in lists:
            if not l: continue
            head = l[0]
            if not any(head in o[1:] for o in lists):   # head not in any tail
                break
        else:
            raise TypeError("no consistent MRO")
        result.append(head)
        lists = [[x for x in l if x is not head] for l in lists]
    return result

class A: pass
class B(A): pass
class C(A): pass
class D(B, C): pass
print([k.__name__ for k in c3(D)])
print([k.__name__ for k in D.__mro__])
try:
    class Q1(A, B): pass
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

followUps:
The MRO is D, B, C, A, object.

Steps by C3: start with D, then merge [B, A, object], [C, A, object] and [B, C]. B is the head of the first list and appears in no tail, so take it. Next A is a head, but it is in the tail of [C, A, object], so skip it and take C. Then A, then object. Check with D.__mro__. A comes after both B and C, which is why super() in B can reach C before A.

Depth-first lookup visits a shared base too early and can bypass a more specific override in another branch, so it is wrong for diamonds.

Example: D(B, C) with A as the common base, and C overrides a method of A. Depth-first goes D, B, A and finds A's version, never seeing C's override. C3 puts A after both B and C, so the more specific C wins. C3 also guarantees monotonic order and makes super() cooperative.

code.title: classmethod factory vs staticmethod

followUps:
Because Date(...) is hard-coded, a subclass calling the factory gets a plain Date back, not itself.

Example: MyDate.from_string('2024-3-9') returns a Date if the body says return Date(...), so any methods added by MyDate are missing. Writing return cls(...) with @classmethod returns a MyDate automatically. It is a quiet bug because the code still runs.

Return Self from typing (Python 3.11 and newer) so type checkers know a subclass call returns the subclass.

from typing import Self

class Date:
    @classmethod
    def from_string(cls, s: str) -> Self:
        return cls(*map(int, s.split('-')))

Before 3.11, use a bound TypeVar: T = TypeVar('T', bound='Date') with cls: type[T] and -> T. Annotations have no runtime cost.

code.title: Duck typing with a Protocol, EAFP vs LBYL

followUps:
EAFP means "easier to ask forgiveness than permission": just try the operation and catch the exception. LBYL means "look before you leap": check first with an if.

EAFP is the Python default and avoids races, e.g. try: v = d[k] except KeyError. LBYL is better when the failure is common and the check is cheap, when a failure would have side effects half-way through, or when the check is the whole point, like validating user input before a file write.

It checks only that the required attribute names exist on the object; it does not check signatures, argument counts, types or return values.

Example: a class with area = 5 (a number, not a method) still passes isinstance(x, HasArea) when the protocol declares area(). The check is also slower than a normal isinstance, because it scans attributes. Use static checkers (mypy, pyright) for the real signature check.

code.title: Composition with a swappable engine; Square breaks Rectangle

followUps:
Square inheriting Rectangle breaks Liskov because code written for rectangles assumes width and height change independently, and a square cannot honour that.

Example: a function does r.w = 5; r.h = 2 and expects area 10. If Square keeps both sides equal, setting w also changes h, so you get 4 or 25, not 10. The fix is to not make Square a subtype of a mutable Rectangle: use a common Shape with area(), or make both immutable.

A mixin is a small class that adds one reusable behaviour and is meant to be combined with others by multiple inheritance, not used alone.

Example: class JsonMixin: def to_json(self): return json.dumps(self.__dict__) then class User(JsonMixin, Base). It is a middle road: you share code without a deep tree. Keep mixins stateless, give them no __init__ of their own, put them before the main base in the bases list, and use super() if they override anything.

code.title: Name mangling and a property for encapsulation

followUps:
It raises AttributeError, because Python rewrote the stored name to _ClassName__balance when the class was built.

You can still read it as obj._Account__balance (assuming the class is named Account), or find it in vars(obj). This shows mangling prevents accidental clashes in subclasses, not deliberate access. Inside the class body, self.__balance works because the compiler applies the same rewrite there.

Switch when you need to add validation, computation or logging on access without changing how callers use it (obj.x stays the same).

Example: start with self.age = age. Later you need age to be non-negative: rename the stored value to _age and add a @property with a setter that raises ValueError for negatives. No caller changes. So do not write getters and setters up front; start plain and upgrade only when a rule appears.

code.title: MinStack with O(1) push, pop, top and min

followUps:
Yes, store only the differences from the current minimum, so one stack of numbers plus one min variable is enough, giving O(1) extra space.

push(v): if empty: min=v; push(0)
  else: push(v-min); if v<min: min=v
pop(): d=pop(); if d<0: min=min-d
  # top: d>=0 ? min+d : min

Example: push 5, 3: stack stores 0, -2 and min is 3. Pop: d=-2 is negative, so the old min is 3-(-2)=5. Every operation is O(1). In Python the numbers are unbounded, so there is no overflow.

Protect every operation with one lock, because push and pop each touch two lists and another thread could see them half-updated.

import threading
self._lock = threading.Lock()
def push(self, v):
    with self._lock:
        ...  # update items and mins

All methods, including get_min, take the same lock, so the invariant holds whenever the lock is free. Operations stay O(1), plus a small lock cost. A single lock is simple; use a lock-free design only if you measure contention.

code.title: Monkey-patching a method and the super() cell error

followUps:
Changing P.hi does nothing to C objects that already have their own hi in C.__dict__; they still use C's version, which is now the lambda.

Example: after P.hi = lambda self: 'P2', P().hi() and any subclass without its own hi return 'P2', but C().hi() still returns 'X'. If you instead delete C's entry (del C.hi), the lookup falls through to P and returns 'P2'. Lookup stops at the first class in the MRO that defines the name.

Zero-argument super() relies on a hidden __class__ cell that the compiler creates only for functions written inside a class body that use super or __class__. A function defined elsewhere has no such cell.

Example: def f(self): return super().hi() at module level, then C.hi = f, raises RuntimeError: super(): __class__ cell not found when called. Fix it by writing super(C, self).hi() explicitly.

code.title: ABC vs Protocol vs register

followUps:
Yes. An abstract method may have a body, and subclasses reach it with super(), so the abstract part forces an override while the base still offers default logic.

class Base(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def run(self):
        return "setup"
class Job(Base):
    def run(self):
        return super().run() + " job"

Job().run() gives 'setup job'. The subclass must still define run, or instantiating it raises TypeError.

Through __subclasshook__, a class method on the ABC that isinstance and issubclass call to decide membership by checking for methods, so inheritance is not needed.

Example: Iterable.__subclasshook__ returns True when the class defines __iter__. So isinstance(MyClass(), Iterable) is True with no inheritance. You can also add classes explicitly with ABC.register(cls). It only checks names, not signatures.

Static linters catch some of these, and the rest need tests. Ruff RUF012 flags mutable class attributes without ClassVar, B006 flags mutable default arguments, and PLR0913 flags too many arguments.

Mypy and pyright catch missing super().__init__ arguments, wrong override signatures (with --strict or the override checks), and abstract classes being instantiated. They cannot judge whether an is-a relation is right or whether invariants hold, so those still need human review and tests.

Explain the refactor with a concrete failing example, not a rule, and keep it kind: the aim is to show the risk, not to blame the teammate or the AI.

Example: "This subclass shares a list between all instances: I created two objects, appended to one, and the other changed too. Here is the 5-line test." Then show the smaller design (a function, dataclass or composition), say what it removes (two classes, one risk), and offer to pair on it. A failing test persuades better than a style opinion.
